rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s messengers are generally first supported by the young: elders are constrained by custom, while youth accept despite worldly consequences; Moses’ tyrannical, ethnically foreign rulers made such courage essential.
rows.anchor: In the case of messengers, God’s established practice has been that in the early stages only the young generally supported them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accepting a prophet’s report as true is distinct from obeying and submitting to it; some Israelite youths had reached only the first stage, so Moses taught them faith’s essence.
rows.anchor: The former means a person’s claim or information given is accepted as true.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the young people’s progeny: they feared Pharaoh and their own chiefs would retaliate, while Israelite elders sympathized with Moses but would not risk their children.
rows.anchor: these young individuals feared the Pharaoh that he may target them because of siding with Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith entails trusting God, and trust entails fully consigning oneself to Him; this is the meaning of Islam.
rows.anchor: the essential consequence of faith is trust in God and the essential consequence of this trust is that a person fully consigns himself to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ companions understood trust as readiness to risk their lives for God’s cause, not withdrawal into seclusion.
rows.anchor: trust does not mean to isolate one’s self in seclusion but to endanger one’s life for the cause of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prayer asks God not to let enemies oppress them into abandoning their religion; meeting trust’s demands also requires resolve and continual supplication for help.
rows.anchor: God should not give their enemies so much respite that they let loose on them so much oppression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses prayed for God’s help in achieving the goal of liberating the Israelites through a successful migration.
rows.anchor: This supplication was to ask for His help to succeed in migration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is the strategy for acquiring the patience and trust taught earlier; the same directive was given to Muhammad and his companions during hardship in Mecca.
rows.anchor: This verse states the strategy through which patience and trust – on which they were instructed earlier – can be acquired.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israelite revival began by restoring collective worship: they were told to pray together and designate houses as mosques, since they could not all gather in one place.
rows.anchor: they were asked to show diligence in praying in congregation and for this some houses should be regarded as mosques

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Israelites were spread throughout Egypt and could not gather in one place, multiple mosques were established.
rows.anchor: it was not possible for the Israelites to gather at one place from all parts of Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author infers that Moses’ and Aaron’s homes served as a temporary central qiblah for nearby followers; after migration the Ark served until the Bayt al-Muqaddas was built.
rows.anchor: these houses were given the status of temporary qiblah in the transitional period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s glad tidings concern believers who persevere in His cause and pray diligently: He grants perseverance and success in both worlds; Israel’s fulfillment appears in 10:93.
rows.anchor: God will make such people persevere and grant them success both in this world and the in the next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses prayed against Pharaoh and his people after losing hope in their belief, as Noah had prayed against the adversaries of his nation.
rows.anchor: It was at this stage when Noah (sws) had prayed for the adversaries of this nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger is the final means of conclusively conveying truth; a nation that still rejects it after a respite is beyond hope and will be destroyed, since worldly life develops capacities rather than evil.
rows.anchor: a messenger is the last means of conclusive communication of the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in Moses’ prayer marks consequence: Pharaoh’s God-given wealth would make him rebellious rather than grateful, so Moses asks that he receive no further respite.
rows.anchor: Here the letter ل expresses the consequence and fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Pharaoh’s people demanded a sign of punishment before believing, Moses prayed for their stubborn demand to be fulfilled after he had lost hope in their faith.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) supplicated before God to fulfil their stubborn demand after he had totally lost hope in they professing faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepted the prayer after Moses and Aaron had fully discharged their preaching and warning responsibilities, then commanded them to persevere.
rows.anchor: Since the responsibility of preaching and warning that was imposed on Moses (sws) and Aaron (sws) had been fulfilled in the best possible way, their prayer was accepted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Aaron must witness the rebels’ fate without sympathy or intercession and must not let the rebels’ corrupt thinking infect them.
rows.anchor: Seeing their horrific end, no sympathy should arise in them nor hould they say any words of recommendation in their favour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning parallels God’s commands to Noah and to Muhammad with his companions; although the messenger is addressed, the direction also reaches his followers, as the address shifts from singular to plural in Hūd.
rows.anchor: On such an occasion, a messenger is apparently addressed; however, the direction of address is towards others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites’ crossing displays God’s special care: the sea gave them a route across, and that same route drowned Pharaoh and his army.
rows.anchor: the very path which the sea provided to the Israelites to cross the sea was the one passing through which the Pharaoh and his army drowned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s pursuit was especially tyrannical because he had first allowed the Israelites to leave, then revoked that permission and chased them.
rows.anchor: after a long conflict, the Pharaoh himself had given the Israelites the permission to go. After that, he recanted and followed them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s profession of faith while drowning depicts helplessness: tyrants acknowledge the truth when seized, but this late acknowledgment bears no fruit.
rows.anchor: When tyrants and despots are seized by God, they are overcome with such type of complete helplessness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke asking whether Pharaoh believes only now may describe his state rather than words actually spoken.
rows.anchor: It is not necessary that the words: “is it now? though before this, you kept showing defiance and were among those who spread disorder” were actually spoken.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea cast Pharaoh’s corpse ashore as an example for later generations; Egyptian mummification preserved bodies, though archaeologists may dispute whether the museum mummy is this Pharaoh, and the Qur’an’s account is more reliable than their conjectures.
rows.anchor: the sea did not accept the corpse of the Pharaoh. In fact, in order to make an example out of it, it threw it out.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s body became a sign even for later rulers, but recognizing its lesson requires the rare gift of insight.
rows.anchor: God made his dead body an exemplary sign for even the Pharaohs of today but this needs eyes for observation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for providing a dwelling means establishing a place; its attachment to “dar sidq” conveys stability and strength, implying political authority in the chosen land.
rows.anchor: means “to provide a place of dwelling” and its annexure towards

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite receiving God’s favors, Israel’s disputes over His religion and Book showed ingratitude and caused them to lose the guidance they had received.
rows.anchor: They created various types of differences in them and thereby lost the guidance they had received.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel’s religious disputes after receiving knowledge and blessings show ingratitude; their disputes over God’s religion and Book cost them guidance, leaving them culpably confused in broad daylight.
rows.anchor: These words show that it was not in the darkness of night that they could not find the way; on the contrary, it was in broad day light that they faltered.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that God will judge their disputes is a threat: their religious fraud and concealment will be exposed, and each person punished according to his crimes.
rows.anchor: every thing will come to light and every person will be punished in accordance with the extent of his crimes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section first warns and rebukes rejecters, assuring the Prophet not to hesitate or grieve; earlier-scripture recipients can corroborate the revelation.
rows.anchor: First the rejected are warned and rebuked by addressing the Prophet (sws): none of their ways should cause any hesitancy in him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section then says signs will not make those already facing God’s judgment believe, recalls Jonah’s nation as the lone historical exception, and insists that God wants freely chosen faith rather than compulsion or demanded miracles.
rows.anchor: God has great liking for people accepting faith but He wants that they profess faith with freedom of choice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should reflect on signs in the inner and outer world; those demanding punishment should wait, as the Prophet does, while God delivers messengers and believers.
rows.anchor: Those who need signs should reflect on the signs of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes with the Prophet’s monotheistic declaration, a final disavowal of disbelief and polytheism that ends hope of compromise.
rows.anchor: This declaration is like the last declaration of acquittal from the religion of disbelief and polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording addresses the Prophet, but its anger is aimed at obstinate rejecters, who are not considered worthy of direct address; a united rejection of obvious truth could unsettle a sincere person, so the verse reassures him.
rows.anchor: At times, the apparent address is to the Prophet (sws) but the anger found in it is actually directed towards the rejecters.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Quraysh undervalue the Qur’an, the Prophet can ask earlier-scripture readers, who will corroborate it; the verse urges righteous People of the Book to make known the truth they already know.
rows.anchor: The verse encourages the righteous that the time has come that they should introduce this truth they know to people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assurance to the Prophet parallels Hūd 11:17, where prior scripture and a further witness support the truth of the Qur’an and distinguish people of insight from rejecters.
rows.anchor: Here the manner in which the Prophet (sws) has been assured is the same as in Sūrah Hūd thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As stated in 10:33, those who remain blind and deaf despite clear truth have sealed hearts and will not seek faith; belief after seeing punishment has no weight before God.
rows.anchor: sealed are the hearts of those who remain blind and deaf in spite of the truth being evident to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s people are the only nation that believed before punishment and benefited; this reassures the Prophet while warning Quraysh that their respite is nearly over but they can still follow that example.
rows.anchor: The time of their respite is about to expire. If they do not pay heed, they will meet the same fate as many other nations of the world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad’s nation did not suffer a decisive destruction like ‘Ād or Thamūd: most capable people gradually entered Islam, while only miscreants remained outside and were killed in battles.
rows.anchor: Most of his people who had the ability, in fact, gradually entered the folds of Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God wants people to believe through intellect and conscience, not force; He could have made everyone believe, but the Prophet’s duty was only to convey the message, and rejecters answer for their choice.
rows.anchor: God really likes people to profess faith but on the condition they do so in the light of their intellect and conscience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith comes by God’s permission and grace, which is acquired by using God-given intellect; those who refuse reason have their insight clouded and follow base desires.
rows.anchor: God casts filth on the insight of those who do not use their intellect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs and miracles throughout the heavens and earth answer deniers’ demand for signs, but only those who intend to benefit can gain from them.
rows.anchor: The heavens and the earth are replete with signs and miracles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs and warnings help only those who intend to believe; “warnings” especially means signs God sends to instill fear.
rows.anchor: warnings” here refer specially refer to signs which are sent by God to strike fear in the hearts of people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If rejecters await the punishments of earlier nations, they should keep waiting: only God can bring punishment, while the Prophet sees its causes gradually arise and waits too.
rows.anchor: it is not the authority of the Prophet (sws) to bring such a punishment. Only God has this authority.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Decisive punishment destroys all except God’s messengers and their believers; this warns Quraysh that God will seize them and protect believers according to His established practice.
rows.anchor: When the Almighty sends such a decisive punishment, only His messengers and those who profess faith in them are protected from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This protection rule concerns punishment of messenger-rejecting nations; ordinary reminder trials affect believers and disbelievers alike, though believers benefit and disbelievers lose their excuse.
rows.anchor: General trials which inflict people to remind them encompass both believers and disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage has the Prophet declare exclusive worship of God and refuse invoking other deities; pressure from disbelievers cannot soften his stance.
rows.anchor: A decisive declaration is made here from the tongue of the Prophet (sws). If the disbelievers think that by pressurizing him, they can soften his stance
